title: What are the EPA certification requirements for restricted use pesticide applicators?
description: 40 CFR Part 171 explained: the 2017 certification rule, applicator categories, exam standards, 5 year recertification and state plan implementation dates.
shortAnswer: Under 40 CFR Part 171, revised by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in a rule effective March 6, 2017, anyone who uses or supervises the use of a restricted use pesticide must be certified under an EPA-approved state, tribal or federal plan, or work under the direct supervision of a certified applicator. Certifications expire after at most five years, applicators must be at least 18, and noncertified applicators need training within the previous 12 months.
keyTakeaways: Part 171 sets minimum federal standards. Certification itself is issued by certifying authorities (states, tribes, territories and some federal agencies) under plans EPA approves.

The 2017 rule took effect March 6, 2017. Certifying authorities had to submit revised plans by March 4, 2020, and older plans stayed in effect until EPA approved the revision or November 4, 2023, whichever came first.
Each approved plan carries its own implementation schedule, so the date a given requirement bites depends on the jurisdiction's approved plan, not on a single national date.

Commercial and private applicator certifications expire five years after issuance unless the applicator is recertified by exam or approved continuing education; a certifying authority may set a shorter period.

Noncertified applicators working under direct supervision must have completed qualifying training within the last 12 months and equipment instruction within the last 12 months, with records kept two years.
jurisdiction: United States (federal minimum standards, implemented through state, tribal and federal agency certification plans)
regulator: US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Pesticide Programs, with state, tribal and federal certifying authorities
appliesTo: Commercial applicators who use or supervise the use of restricted use pesticides
Private applicators, such as farmers and ranchers, using restricted use pesticides to produce agricultural commodities
Noncertified applicators using restricted use pesticides under the direct supervision of a certified applicator
State, tribal, territorial and federal agencies that administer certification plans

sections.heading: Who needs to be a certified pesticide applicator?

blocks.text: Anyone who uses or supervises the use of a restricted use pesticide must be certified, or must use it under the direct supervision of a certified applicator. Under [40 CFR 171.1](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/171.1), a person is a certified applicator for the purposes of the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) only if they hold a certification issued under an approved plan that is currently valid in the pertinent jurisdiction.

"Use" is defined broadly in [40 CFR 171.3](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/171.3). It covers mixing and loading, applying (including supervising a noncertified applicator), and related activities such as transporting or storing opened containers, cleaning equipment, and disposing of excess pesticide and containers. A person who only mixes and loads is still using the pesticide.

Federal certification applies to restricted use pesticides. EPA's [certification standards page](https://www.epa.gov/pesticide-worker-safety/revised-certification-standards-pesticide-applicators) notes that many state agencies require certification to apply any pesticide commercially, whether or not it is restricted use, and that the stronger standards apply in those states too.

blocks.title: Transition status
blocks.text: As at November 2026, EPA's page reports that 67 of 68 proposed plan revisions from state, territory, tribal and federal certifying authorities have been approved. Each approved plan has an implementation schedule agreed with EPA, so applicators are not required to meet every new requirement on the day the plan is approved. Check the approved plan for your jurisdiction.

sections.heading: When did the 2017 rule take effect in each state?

blocks.text: Part 171 became effective on March 6, 2017, but most of its standards reach applicators through revised state, tribal and federal agency plans. [40 CFR 171.5](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/171.5) sets the transition: plans approved before March 6, 2017 remained approved until March 4, 2020, and a certifying authority that submitted a proposed revision by that date kept its existing plan in effect until EPA approved or rejected the revision or until November 4, 2023, whichever was earlier.

The November 4, 2023 end date came from an August 2022 amendment (87 FR 50965), which EPA's page explains as an extension driven by the challenges certifying authorities faced and the COVID-19 public health emergency. Where EPA has approved a revised plan, section 171.5(d) lets the old plan remain in effect as specified in that approval, which is how the per plan implementation schedules work.

For a training manager, the practical answer to "when does this apply" is therefore the implementation schedule in the jurisdiction's EPA-approved plan. EPA lists approved plans and has published batch Federal Register notices of approvals.

Commercial applicators must pass a written examination covering core standards and the standards for each category they seek. Under [40 CFR 171.103](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/171.103), the exam must be presented and answered in writing, proctored by a person designated by the certifying authority who is not seeking certification at that session, and taken with valid government-issued photo identification as proof of identity and age. Candidates must be monitored throughout and may use only reference materials approved by the certifying authority and supplied by the proctor.

The core standards in section 171.103(c) have ten areas: label and labeling comprehension (including the difference between mandatory and advisory labeling language), safety, environment, pests, pesticides, equipment, application methods, laws and regulations, responsibilities of supervisors of noncertified applicators, and professionalism. Category exams in section 171.101 cover 15 commercial categories, including agricultural (crop and livestock), forest, ornamental and turf, seed treatment, aquatic, right-of-way, industrial, institutional and structural, public health, regulatory, demonstration and research, two predator control categories, and three application method categories added in 2017: soil fumigation, non-soil fumigation and aerial pest control.

Private applicators may be certified by an exam meeting the same administration standards or by a non-examination training program approved by the certifying authority under section 171.105(h). Private applicators using soil fumigation, non-soil fumigation, aerial application or the predator control products need additional category certification. See [criterion-referenced versus norm-referenced assessment](/compare/criterion-referenced-vs-norm-referenced-assessment) for how competency exams of this kind are designed.

sections.heading: What are the age and recertification rules?

blocks.text: Commercial and private applicators must be at least 18 years old under sections 171.103(a)(1) and 171.105(g). Certification expires five years after issuance unless the applicator is recertified, and a certifying authority may set a shorter period under [40 CFR 171.107](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/171.107). To avoid a gap, recertification must be completed before the current certification expires.

Recertification is by written examination meeting the section 171.103(a)(2) standards or by a continuing education program in the approved plan. Continuing education must be sufficient in quantity, content and quality to keep the applicator at the competency level required, each course or event must be approved by the certifying authority, and online or distance courses must include a process to verify successful completion.

The completion verification rule matters for digital training providers: a click-through module without identity and completion checks will not satisfy it. The guide on [setting mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) covers scheduling recertification ahead of expiry.

sections.heading: What training do noncertified applicators need?

blocks.text: Before a noncertified applicator uses a restricted use pesticide under direct supervision, the certified applicator must ensure they meet one of four qualifications in [40 CFR 171.201(c)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/171.201): training under section 171.201(d) within the last 12 months, Worker Protection Standard handler training under 40 CFR 170.501 within the last 12 months, a certifying authority program that meets or exceeds the standard, or current certification that does not cover the type of application or jurisdiction.

The noncertified applicator must also have been instructed within the last 12 months in safe operation of any equipment used for mixing, loading, transferring or applying, and must be at least 18. The exception is 16 for a noncertified applicator supervised by a private applicator who is an immediate family member, provided the product is not a fumigant, sodium cyanide or sodium fluoroacetate and the application is not aerial.

The section 171.201(d) program has 25 required topics, delivered orally from written materials or audiovisually by a trainer present throughout. Beyond personal protection and decontamination, it covers label format including the restricted use product statement, and the supervising applicator's duties to give site-specific instructions, ensure label access, provide clean required protective equipment, check equipment before each day of use, and keep a means of immediate communication.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps the Part 171 core and category competency standards into a framework of concepts and assessment points, so continuing education content can be checked against the competency it is meant to maintain. When a jurisdiction's approved plan sets additional requirements, those are added as a layer on the federal framework rather than as a separate course set.

faqs.q: Does Worker Protection Standard handler training qualify someone to apply restricted use pesticides?
faqs.a: It qualifies a person to use restricted use pesticides as a noncertified applicator under the direct supervision of a certified applicator, provided it was completed within the last 12 months, together with equipment instruction and the age requirement. It does not make the person a certified applicator.

faqs.q: Can recertification be done entirely online?
faqs.a: Part 171 allows continuing education programs approved by the certifying authority, and section 171.107(b)(2)(iii) requires online or distance courses to include a process to verify successful completion. Whether a particular online course counts depends on the certifying authority's approved plan.

faqs.q: What records must a commercial applicator keep for noncertified applicators?
faqs.a: Before allowing use, the commercial applicator must create or verify a record of each noncertified applicator's qualification. For training under section 171.201(d), it includes printed name and signature, date, trainer name and training title. The records must be accessible at the principal place of business for two years from the date of use.

Certifying authorities issue them: EPA, or a state, tribal or federal agency operating an EPA-approved certification plan. EPA's page lists approved federal agency plans and tribal plans, and notes that all 50 states, the District of Columbia, tribes, territories and federal agencies administer certification programs.
